title: Managing battery state of charge to extend storage lifespan
subtitle: Keeping a home battery within its recommended charge window to slow capacity degradation
excerpt: A home battery lasts longest when you keep it between 20% and 90% state of charge most of the time and avoid holding it at 100% for extended periods. Most battery management systems enforce these limits automatically, but understanding the settings lets you balance daily self-consumption against long-term battery health.
sourceNotes: Battery technology research on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and NMC degradation mechanisms; BYD Battery-Box and Growatt documentation; Tesla Powerwall support guidance on charge settings.

glossaryTerms.definition: The current charge level of a battery expressed as a percentage of its total capacity. 0% = fully discharged; 100% = fully charged.
A home energy storage system that stores electricity — typically from solar PV — for use at night or during high-tariff periods.
The percentage of a battery's capacity that has been used in a single cycle. A 10 kWh battery discharged from 90% to 20% SoC has a DoD of 70%.

content.text: Lithium battery capacity decreases with each charge cycle. The rate of decrease depends heavily on how the battery is used. Charging to 100% and discharging to 0% repeatedly — full

systems enforce maximum and minimum charge limits through the battery management system (BMS), but the default settings vary by product.

Lithium iron phosphate (LFP): used in most current home batteries (BYD, GivEnergy, Pylontech). More tolerant of full charges and discharges than NMC; rated for 3,000–6,000 cycles to 80% capacity at full DoD. Less heat-sensitive than NMC.

Nickel manganese cobalt (NMC): used in Tesla Powerwall 2 and some older systems. More energy-dense than LFP but degrades faster at high SoC. Tesla recommends keeping Powerwall below 100% unless you have backup reserve requirements.

For daily self-consumption use, set the maximum charge limit to 90–95% and the minimum discharge limit to 10–15%. This extends expected cycle life by 20–40% compared to full cycles, at the cost of roughly 10–15% of usable capacity. The trade-off is usually worth it over a 10-year system life.

Exception: if you are on a time-of-use tariff and charging from the grid at off-peak rates to use at peak, charging to 100% for planned evening use is acceptable occasionally. Holding a battery at 100% overnight repeatedly — with no plan to discharge it before the next solar day — accelerates degradation.
Where to find the charge settings
GivEnergy / Solis / Sofar: accessible via the inverter's web portal or the manufacturer app. Look for "charge upper limit" and "discharge lower limit" settings.
Tesla Powerwall: set the "reserve for power outages" percentage in the Tesla app; the system will charge to 100% only when grid backup is needed beyond the reserve.
Sonnen: managed automatically by the BMS; user can set a reserve percentage.

High ambient temperature accelerates degradation. A battery in an uninsulated south-facing garage that reaches 35–40°C in summer degrades measurably faster than one in a cool utility room. If your battery is in a hot location, consider keeping the maximum charge limit at 80% in summer.

rows.symptom: Battery capacity seems to have dropped significantly after two years
rows.cause: System has been cycling to 100% and 0% daily; or high-temperature exposure
rows.fix: Check the cycle count in the monitoring app; adjust charge limits to 20–90% going forward. Most manufacturers' warranties are voided only by operating outside the recommended temperature range, not by full cycling.

rows.symptom: Battery not charging beyond 80% even though limit is set to 90%
rows.cause: BMS is in a protective mode due to cell imbalance or temperature compensation
rows.fix: Allow the battery to run a full calibration cycle (manufacturer-specific: usually charge to 100% then discharge to 10% under normal load). If the problem persists, contact the manufacturer.
